items.prompt: What is the author’s principal point?
options: The median always provides all necessary information
Household water use cannot be measured accurately

items.title: The Problem with an Average
items.passage:
An average can summarize a large collection of measurements in a convenient number. If a town reports its average household water use, residents can compare their own use with a general pattern. Yet the summary does not reveal how much households differ from one another.
Consider two streets with the same average consumption. On one street, nearly every household uses a similar amount. On the other, several households use very little while a few use extremely large amounts. A campaign based on the average alone might treat both streets alike even though the opportunities for reducing consumption differ.
Researchers therefore examine the distribution of measurements as well as a central value. They may report the median, the value in the middle of an ordered list, or describe how widely observations are spread. These measures answer different questions. The median is less influenced by a small number of extreme observations, but it does not make the extremes irrelevant to planning.
The most useful summary depends on the decision being made. A water supplier estimating total demand may need information that differs from what a household needs when comparing itself with similar neighbors. Averages are not inherently misleading; problems arise when a convenient summary is asked to answer a question it was not designed to address.

items.prompt: Why might adding flower seeds fail in a nutrient-rich meadow?
options: All flowering plants need permanently shaded conditions
Fast-growing grasses can deprive seedlings of light
The seeds necessarily come from nearby populations
Nutrients prevent every plant from producing seeds
items.explanation: Grasses benefit from nutrients and shade out smaller plants.
items.title: Restoring a Meadow
items.passage:
Restoring a damaged meadow involves more than scattering seeds. Plants interact with the soil, available light and neighboring species, so the same seed mixture may succeed at one location and fail at another. Restoration teams begin by investigating why the original plant community declined.
In some meadows, nutrients added during earlier agricultural use favor rapidly growing grasses. Those grasses can shade out smaller flowering plants. Adding more flower seeds does little if the seedlings cannot obtain enough light. Managers may remove cut vegetation after mowing so that nutrients are gradually carried away rather than returned to the soil as the material decomposes.
Timing is also important. Cutting a meadow too early can prevent desirable plants from producing seeds. Cutting too late may allow aggressive species to dominate. A schedule must reflect local conditions and the life cycles of the plants that managers hope to encourage.
Progress is usually uneven. Some species establish quickly, while others arrive slowly from nearby populations or require conditions that take years to develop. Monitoring helps managers distinguish a temporary delay from a persistent obstacle. Restoration is therefore an ongoing process of observing and adjusting, not a single intervention with an immediately visible final result. A visually green field may still be far from the diverse meadow that a project intends to recover.

lower.prompt: What is the passage’s main claim?
options: Successful tool lending requires organization and care as well as equipment
A large collection automatically meets every community need
Members should buy every item they borrow
Tool libraries have no function beyond storing objects
lower.explanation: Demand, trust, maintenance and knowledge support shared access.
lower.title: Borrowing as a Social Arrangement
lower.passage:
A tool library lends equipment that people may need only occasionally. Instead of buying a drill for a single project, a member can borrow one and return it for someone else to use. This arrangement can reduce the number of products that must be owned individually, but its success depends on more than having shelves full of tools.
Demand is uneven. Many members may want gardening equipment on the same weekend, while another item remains unused for months. Keeping records of loans helps organizers decide which tools to buy in greater numbers and which purchases would add little value. A rarely borrowed tool is not necessarily useless, however; it may meet an unusual need that would otherwise be costly to satisfy.
Trust and responsibility matter as well. Members need clear instructions about safe use, cleaning and reporting faults. If damaged tools return to the shelf without inspection, the next borrower may face inconvenience or danger. Maintenance work is therefore part of the lending service rather than an optional extra.
Tool libraries also provide opportunities for people to exchange practical knowledge. A demonstration can help a borrower use unfamiliar equipment confidently. The library is consequently both a collection of objects and a system of relationships, information and ongoing care that makes shared access possible.

higher.prompt: What primarily shapes the formation of dunes?
options: The growth of roots without any transported material
A single event that fixes the landscape permanently
The movement and deposition of sand by wind
The complete absence of moving air
higher.explanation: Transport and deposition are the central processes.
higher.title: A Landscape Shaped by Wind
higher.passage:
Sand dunes can appear permanent when viewed during a brief visit, yet they are continually shaped by movement. Wind lifts or pushes grains along the surface, and grains may accumulate where the moving air loses energy. A dune’s form reflects both this transport and the obstacles the wind encounters.
Vegetation can alter the process. Stems and leaves slow air near the ground, encouraging sand to settle. Roots help hold the accumulated material in place. The resulting pattern is not simply a case of plants stopping all movement. Some dune plants can grow upward as sand gathers around them, gradually influencing the shape of the dune.
Human activity can interrupt these interactions. Repeated footsteps may damage plants and create a bare path through which sand moves more readily. A small gap can widen as wind carries additional material through it. Boardwalks are sometimes installed to concentrate visitors on a durable route while reducing damage to neighboring vegetation.
Management must still account for the ecological role of movement. Completely stabilizing every dune would not necessarily protect all the organisms that depend on these environments. Some species need open, shifting sand. Understanding dunes therefore requires attention to both persistence and change, and conservation decisions must consider which processes support the particular habitat being managed.

items.title: What a Replica Can Teach

stimulus.title: What a Replica Can Teach
stimulus.script:
A replica in a museum is sometimes treated as a poor substitute for a real object. But a carefully made replica can support learning that would be impossible with a fragile original. Visitors may handle it, inspect details closely or test how a tool would have been held.
The value depends partly on the purpose of the replica. A copy made to show color may use a different material from the original. That could be appropriate for visual teaching but misleading in a demonstration about weight. Museums need to explain which properties the replica reproduces and which it does not.
Making a replica can also become a form of investigation. A craftsperson trying to reproduce a historical technique may discover difficulties not apparent in a finished object. However, successfully making one possible version does not prove that people in the past used exactly that procedure. Other methods may have produced a similar result.
So replicas are neither automatically worthless nor automatically equivalent to originals. They are tools whose usefulness depends on transparent choices. Clear labels, explicit purposes and attention to limitations allow them to expand access while preserving the distinction between a surviving historical object and a modern interpretation of it.

stimulus.title: Why Young Trees Need Follow-up
stimulus.script:
Planting a young tree is a visible event, easy to photograph and count. Whether it develops into a mature tree depends on what happens afterward. Water, soil conditions and damage during its first years can influence whether the initial investment produces a lasting result.
One challenge is that the roots may occupy a much smaller area than the future crown suggests. During dry weather, a young tree may not yet reach enough moisture. A planting program needs a realistic watering plan rather than assuming that rainfall will always supply what is needed. Local soil and drainage also matter; more water is not the right answer in every situation.
Monitoring helps identify problems before they become irreversible. A support tie that was helpful at planting can become restrictive as the trunk grows. Inspecting it later is part of care, not evidence that the planting was a mistake. Similarly, replacing a failed tree without examining the cause may simply repeat the failure.
This is why evaluating a planting program only by its first-day totals can be misleading. Survival and growth provide information about its longer-term success. A smaller number of well-supported trees may eventually supply more useful canopy than a much larger number that receives no continuing care.

Access is a relationship between an available service and the circumstances of the people who might use it.

options: Survey timing can influence apparent differences between sites

higher.explanation: The talk examines a timing-related interpretation problem.
higher.title: The Timing of a Biological Survey

stimulus.title: The Timing of a Biological Survey
stimulus.script:
Imagine comparing two meadows by visiting the first in early spring and the second in midsummer. You find more flowering species at the second site. Does that show it has greater plant diversity? Not necessarily. The timing of the visits may explain part of the difference.
Different species become visible or identifiable at different stages of the year. A plant present underground may not yet have leaves or flowers that make it easy to record. Researchers therefore plan survey dates around the organisms they want to study. Repeated visits can reduce the risk that one brief period is treated as a complete picture.
Weather adds variation within the same calendar dates. A warm season may bring flowering forward, while a cooler season delays it. Simply returning on exactly the same date each year does not guarantee identical biological conditions. Notes about recent weather and growth stages can help interpret comparisons.
The practical lesson is that absence from a survey list is not always evidence of absence from the site. Good survey design links the method and timing to the question. Researchers can still make useful comparisons, but they must identify which differences might reflect the observation process rather than the communities being compared.
